citation.author: Darling, Tom
citation.title: Synthesising Boredom: A Predictive Processing Approach
citation.affiliationNote: Monash Centre for Consciousness & Contemplative Studies

discipline: psychology / cognitive science -- predictive-processing (computational) theory of affect, in explicit dialogue with Heideggerian phenomenology
thesis: Darling identifies a tension between two conceptions of boredom that rarely speak to one another: the psychological literature's dominant view of boredom as an adaptive, self-regulatory emotion, and the phenomenological tradition's view -- following Heidegger -- of boredom as a Grundstimmung, a fundamental mood disclosing 'the predicament of human existence' (Slaby 2010, paraphrased). The paper's stated aim is to use predictive processing (broadly construed, including active inference and the Free Energy Principle) to offer an integrative account of boredom that resolves this tension by (1) formally explaining the psychological 'Goldilocks zone' of optimal engagement and boredom's 'call to action' (Danckert & Elpidorou 2023); (2) naturalising the phenomenological tradition without reducing it away, addressing Elpidorou's own worry that no existing account does justice to both outlooks (2018c, paraphrased); and (3) dissolving the 'unitary vs. plural' debate about boredom's conceptual status by locating emotion and mood at different levels of one predictive hierarchy.
sections: SS1 Introduction: the problem of boredom (pp.1-4) -- stakes the 'problem of boredom' (Svendsen), surveys the psychological self-regulation literature, introduces the Heideggerian mood tradition, and previews the predictive-processing synthesis

SS2 Boredom as a self-regulating emotion (pp.4-6) -- the psychological literature: definition, attention, meaning, exploit/explore switching, the Goldilocks zone, functional theories (incl. Westgate & Wilson's MAC model)
SS3 Heidegger's phenomenology of mood (pp.6-9) -- Grundstimmung, Stimmung/Befindlichkeit, mood as pre-intentional and world-disclosive, mood vs. emotion

SS4 The Predictive Processing Approach, incl. SS4.1 Affective inference (pp.8-13) -- predictive processing/active inference/FEP fundamentals; interoceptive, information-theoretic (valence), and computational (Hesp et al.) accounts of affect; mood as hyperprior (Clark et al.; Kiverstein et al.'s 'feeling of grip')

SS5 Synthesising boredom, with SS5.1 Adaptive boredom, SS5.2 Maladaptive boredom, SS5.3 The existential problem of boredom (pp.12-19) -- the paper's constructive core: boredom-as-emotion tracking error-dynamics, boredom-as-mood as hyperprior, existential escapes/addiction, and the 'sticky hyperprior' account of maladaptive/existential boredom, explicitly analogised to depression
SS6 Concluding remarks (pp.19-20) -- distinguishes interoceptive/emotional/affective inference; restates the synthesis

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: The paper's starting frame and, after the predictive-processing turn, its own reconstructed conclusion: boredom as the 'aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity' (Eastwood et al. 2012, p.483, quoted at p.4), re-derived in SS5.1 as a mechanism tracking the rate of prediction-error reduction relative to an agent's expected rate, catalysing exploit/explore domain-switches.

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: Framed as boredom's central regulatory mechanism: 'the mind may wander' when bored, agents struggling to sustain attention on the present task (citing Danckert & Merrifield 2018; Yakobi et al. 2021); later reframed computationally as a candidate mechanism for precision-estimation, since attention is 'often suggested as a mechanism for controlling precision-estimation' (footnote 10).

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: Named explicitly, though briefly, via the 'mind may wander' phrase; not elaborated as a distinct construct beyond this single mention.

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: A recurring thread: perceived meaninglessness drives boredom's self-regulatory search for engagement in SS2 (citing Van Tilburg & Igou; Chan et al. 2018), and resurfaces in SS5.3 as the affective core of existential boredom, likened to Frankl's 'existential vacuum' (paraphrasing Frankl 1967).

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: Never named as such (no citation of Csikszentmihalyi or 'flow' as a term, though 'flow' appears twice in the reference list only), but functions throughout as boredom's implicit contrast: satisfying activity, 'meaningful engagement,' and the world's 'affective allure' (Krueger & Colombetti) recur as what boredom's absence signals the lack of.

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: Engaged mainly via the 'unitary vs. construct' debate (is boredom 'one or many'?, citing Elpidorou 2021; Tempelaar & Niculescu 2022); predictive processing's own resolution -- that emotion and mood are different hierarchical levels/timescales of one system -- is offered as dissolving rather than adjudicating this state/trait-adjacent question.

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: A light touch: the term itself is not used in Darling's own prose, but the maladaptive-escape discussion in SS5.2 leans on a cluster of boredom-proneness studies (Biolcati et al. 2016, 2018; Blaszczynski et al. 1990; Chou et al. 2018; Watt & Vodanovich 1992) cited for links between boredom and addictive/impulsive behaviour.

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: Engaged thematically (via Grundstimmung and the 'sticky hyperprior'/depression analysis) rather than via FCM's own tripartite vocabulary -- see readings/Reading-of-FCM discussion.

constructs.label: predictive-processing model
constructs.treatment: This source's own THEORY-MODEL apparatus, formally operationalizing boredom's mechanism (prediction error, precision-weighting, hyperpriors) rather than reporting first-party data.

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: Not substantively engaged: appears only obliquely, via mood-as-'momentum' (Eldar et al. 2016), rather than the phenomenology of subjective time dragging.

constructs.label: being-bored-by (1st form)
constructs.treatment: Not discussed at all -- Darling's Heidegger section stays at the level of Grundstimmung generally and never differentiates FCM's three forms.

constructs.label: being-bored-with (2nd form)
constructs.treatment: Not discussed at all -- Darling's Heidegger section stays at the level of Grundstimmung generally and never differentiates FCM's three forms.

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.treatment: Yakobi et al. (2021, 'behavioral and electroencephalographic evidence for reduced attentional control'), Cheyne et al. (2006), Carriere et al. (2008), and Milyavskaya et al. (2019, 'high-powered neurophysiological investigation') all cited as literature evidence for attentional lapses and reward-sensitivity during boredom -- none engaged as first-party data or as an elaborated EEG measure; the Yakobi et al. title is the paper's only EEG-adjacent citation, and its EEG methodology is never itself discussed. No EEG (frontal alpha asymmetry, alpha/theta power, functional connectivity, eyes-open/closed), pupillometry, gaze/fixation, blink, HRV, self-report/survey scale, or ML-classification measure is administered, elaborated, or discussed anywhere in this source, consistent with its status as a theoretical/synthesis article rather than an empirical report.

readings.summary: Darling's engagement with Heidegger operates almost entirely at the level of general phenomenology of mood, drawing primarily on Being and Time (1962) vocabulary (Befindlichkeit, Stimmung, primordial disclosure, 'we are always in a mood') rather than on FCM's specific tripartite analysis. Direct citations to FCM (Heidegger 1995) are limited to exactly two moments: a scene-setting note that Heidegger devoted 'some 130 (originally German) pages' to boredom in FCM, identifying it there as a Grundstimmung (p.6); and two short quotations from FCM p.67 -- moods 'colour our entire existence like an essential background atmosphere,' and moods are a 'fundamental manner and fundamental way of Being' (pp.7-8). No discussion of FCM's tripartite typology (being-bored-by, being-bored-with, profound boredom), no dinner-party or train-station examples, and no section-level (SS19-38) citations to FCM's own architecture appear anywhere.
readings.tag: FAITHFUL-Darling, pp.6-9 (two direct FCM citations only; remainder is Being and Time)

readings.summary: Where Darling's own analysis resonates strongly with FCM's third form is thematically, not citationally: SS5.3's 'sticky hyperprior' account of maladaptive/existential boredom -- rigid precision-estimation such that 'no action policy is appealing' and 'the world itself is boring' -- parallels FCM's profound boredom (the impersonal 'it is boring for one,' total withdrawal of significance), but Darling reaches this territory via Clark, Watson & Friston's (2018) computational model of mood-in-depression and Ratcliffe's phenomenology of depression, not via any citation to FCM's own profound-boredom sections (pp.132-159). This is flagged only as this cluster's own thematic alignment (P/anticipatory-application), not a claim Darling makes about FCM's specific material.
readings.loci: pp.17-19 (thematic parallel only; no FCM citation)

hyperprior (mood as a hyperprior over precision)
three species of affective inference: interoceptive, emotional, affective

James Danckert and Andreas Elpidorou (2023) -- co-authored source of the 'Goldilocks zone' and boredom's 'call to action' framing (p.494), cited among the psychological functional literature

Andreas Elpidorou (2018a, 'The Bored Mind is a Guiding Mind') -- regulatory theory of boredom cited among the self-regulation literature (p.4); read as complementary to, not identical with, Darling's predictive-processing mechanism; corresponds to bor-sec-25 in this cluster
Andreas Elpidorou (2018c, p.177) -- source of the naturalize-without-reducing worry Darling explicitly sets out to answer
Andreas Elpidorou (2021) -- cited on the unitary-vs-plural conceptual-status debate about boredom
Erin Westgate and Timothy Wilson -- MAC (meaning and attentional components) model, surveyed among functional theories in SS2
John Eastwood et al. (2012) -- source of the 'aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity' definition, quoted at p.4
James Danckert and Colleen Merrifield (2018) -- cited on mind-wandering ('the mind may wander') when bored (p.4)
Yakobi, O. et al. (2021) -- behavioral/EEG evidence for reduced attentional control, cited among literature evidence (p.4); title only, methodology not discussed
Cheyne, J.A. et al. (2006) -- cited alongside Carriere et al. and Milyavskaya et al. as literature evidence for attentional lapses/reward-sensitivity during boredom (p.15)
Carriere, J.S.A. et al. (2008) -- cited alongside Cheyne et al. for attentional-lapse evidence (p.15)
Milyavskaya, M. et al. (2019) -- 'high-powered neurophysiological investigation,' cited among literature evidence for reward-sensitivity during boredom (p.15)
Wijnand Van Tilburg and Eric Igou -- meaning-regulation literature cited in SS2's monotony/meaninglessness discussion
Chan, C.S. et al. (2018) -- cited alongside Van Tilburg & Igou on meaninglessness driving boredom's self-regulatory search
Julian Kiverstein et al. (2019, 2020) -- source of the 'feeling of grip' account of mood-as-hyperprior; Darling adopts this as the direct formal analogue of Heideggerian attunement
Andy Clark, Watson, and Karl Friston (2018) -- active-inference account of major depression; source of the 'sticky hyperprior' mechanism Darling analogises to maladaptive/existential boredom
Maxwell Ramstead et al. (2020) -- companion active-inference depression account; source of the 'things that could be done, but not things I can do' quotation (2020, p.27, quoted at p.17)

Martin Heidegger -- Being and Time (1962), primary vocabulary source (Befindlichkeit, Stimmung, primordial disclosure), and The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1995), cited directly only twice (pp.6-8)

Biolcati, R. et al. (2016, 2018); Blaszczynski, A. et al. (1990); Chou, C. et al. (2018); Watt, J.D. and Vodanovich, S.J. (1992) -- boredom-proneness/addiction literature cluster cited in SS5.2 (p.15)
Joel Krueger and Giovanna Colombetti -- source of the 'affective allure' phrase for the world's engaging pull (p.18)
tensions: PRIMARY DEBATE-AXIS ENGAGEMENT (adjacent to, not identical with, the cluster's named 'boredom-as-deficit <-> boredom-as-functional/adaptive' axis grounded in bor-sec-25/26): the psychological functional/self-regulatory account of boredom-as-emotion vs. the Heideggerian phenomenological account of boredom-as-mood (Grundstimmung). Darling's stated aim is not to adjudicate this tension but to dissolve it by locating emotion and mood as different levels/timescales of one predictive hierarchy (pp.2-3, 19-20), explicitly aiming to naturalise the phenomenological tradition 'without reducing it away' (addressing Elpidorou's 2018c worry, paraphrased).

Unitary vs. plural boredom debate (is boredom 'one or many'?, citing Elpidorou 2021; Tempelaar & Niculescu 2022) -- resolved (dissolved rather than adjudicated) by treating emotion and mood as levels of one hierarchy rather than distinct kinds (pp.3, 20).

Adaptive (locally functional) vs. maladaptive/existential (globally dysfunctional) boredom -- existential-escape behaviours (binge eating, drinking, gambling, gaming, pornography, social media) are locally adaptive yet globally maladaptive; explicitly non-pathologizing, since 'the system is functioning largely how it is meant to (biologically)' (p.15, paraphrased).

The 'dark room problem' objection (a pure error-minimiser should seek maximal boredom/inactivity) is explicitly bracketed rather than resolved (p.3, footnote 1) -- an acknowledged but unresolved tension internal to the predictive-processing framework itself.
